title: The Founder Who Became a Verb
hook: Elbridge Gerry signed the Declaration of Independence and served as vice president. He is remembered for a single map he signed in 1812 — and for the insult built from his name.
key_points: Elbridge Gerry was a Massachusetts founder: signer of the Declaration, delegate to the Constitutional Convention, later James Madison's vice president.
As governor in 1812 he approved a state senate map drawn to favor his own party.
A newspaper cartoon likened one contorted district to a salamander; 'Gerry' plus 'salamander' produced 'gerrymander'.
Gerry himself pronounced his name with a hard G — the word almost everyone now says with a soft one.
The word outlived the man: the tactic is over two centuries old and still central to redistricting fights.
content_html: Elbridge Gerry had a serious revolutionary résumé — he signed the Declaration of Independence, sat at the Constitutional Convention (where he declined to sign the finished document), and ended his career as James Madison's vice president. None of that is why anyone says his name today.
extra_html: As NPR's Scott Neuman recounts, in 1812 Gerry was governor of Massachusetts when he approved a state senate map drawn to advantage his own party. One of the resulting districts was so contorted that a newspaper cartoonist drew it as a winged monster, and a wit fused the governor's name with "salamander" to get "gerrymander." The coinage stuck harder than anything Gerry actually did in office. There is even a small linguistic injustice in it: Gerry said his name with a hard G, while the word is now almost universally pronounced with a soft one. The durable lesson is not about one man's reputation but about the incentive he acted on — in any system that elects representatives from geographic districts, the people who draw the boundaries hold real power over the result, which is why two centuries later the fight is still over who gets to hold the pen.

related.hook: Where you draw the lines on a map can decide an election before a single vote is cast — which is exactly what gerrymandering exploits.

flashcards.prompt: Where does the word 'gerrymander' come from?
flashcards.back_html: From Elbridge Gerry, the Massachusetts governor who approved a party-favoring 1812 map, blended with salamander — the shape a newspaper cartoon said one district resembled.

flashcards.prompt: What else was Elbridge Gerry known for besides the map that made his name infamous?

choices.text: He signed the Declaration of Independence and later served as vice president
He was the first chief justice of the Supreme Court
He wrote most of the Federalist Papers

flashcards.explanation_html: Gerry was a prominent revolutionary-era figure and Madison's vice president — the redistricting episode overshadowed all of it.

flashcards.prompt: What does the survival of this 1812 coinage tell you about redistricting?

choices.text: Manipulating district lines is an old, recurring temptation, not a modern invention
District maps were only invented in the 20th century
The practice was outlawed shortly after 1812

flashcards.explanation_html: The word has lasted because the incentive has: whoever draws the lines in a district system can shape the outcome.
